scores.worst_problem: A couple of loops lean on empty abstraction — "Your street decides something bigger" and "Where you buy changes more than that" tease a category without naming a stake, so they pull weaker than the concrete ones like "The bigger bill lands once yearly."
scores.fix: Rewrite the vague loops to name the noun being withheld — e.g. swap "Your street decides something bigger" for "Your street decides your school" and "Where you buy changes more than that" for "Same house, different tax bill."

deck.topic: What surprises Texas transplants (SA, Austin, DFW)
deck.hook: The 47 day stretch nobody warns transplants about.

points.title: The 47 Day Stretch
body: Some Texas summers stack 47 days over 100 degrees.
It changes when you run errands, not if you run them. Mornings and after dark.
points.loop: Cooling is not the expensive part.

points.title: The Water Bill Trap
body: Summer water beats summer electricity for a lot of people here.
Clay soil moves. You water the foundation on a schedule or you pay a repair crew later.
points.loop: The bigger bill lands once yearly.

points.title: No Income Tax, But
body: Texas gets it back through property tax.
Rates swing hard between counties, cities, and school districts. Two nearly identical houses can be taxed very differently.
points.loop: Where you buy changes more than that.

points.title: Commutes That Lie
body: Austin's 20 minute drive is 55 minutes at five o'clock.
DFW feels easy until a toll road or a lake sits between you and work. San Antonio loops back up fast at rush hour.

points.title: School Zoning Shifts
body: Districts here grow fast, so attendance boundaries get redrawn.
The rating follows the boundary, not the house. People buy for a campus and get reassigned two years later.
points.loop: Weekdays are only half the problem.

points.title: Weekends By City
body: From San Antonio and Austin, the Hill Country is under an hour.
From DFW you are driving to lakes and small towns instead. Same state, completely different Saturday.
points.loop: Most people pick the wrong city.

linkedinCaption:
Most people relocating to Texas research the housing market carefully and the daily reality barely at all.

Then they arrive in July.

I put together six things that catch transplants off guard in San Antonio, Austin, and DFW. Not the obvious heat complaint. The specifics. Why summer water bills can outrun electricity. Why clay soil makes foundation watering a maintenance schedule, not a suggestion. How two nearly identical houses land in very different tax situations depending on which taxing entities they sit inside. How fast school attendance boundaries get redrawn in growing districts.

None of it should stop a move. It should shape which neighborhood you choose.

For agents working with out of state buyers: which of these do you find hardest to explain before they see it firsthand?
